title: De altitudine columnarum sub proprio pondere corruentium

deep.reconstruction:
Context: E510 asks how tall a vertical cylindrical column (modelled as an elastic lamina of equal stiffness) can be before it buckles under its own weight. In the preceding sections Euler derived the linearized curve of a heavy elastic lamina with a free top A and gravity as the only load. In modern terms the ordinates are infinitesimal, with EI y''(s) = M(s), where M(s) is the moment of the weight of the part above s about the section at s. Differentiating gives an Airy-type equation for the slope, EI θ'' + q s θ = 0, with s measured from the free top; Euler solves it by series. The resulting infinite curve oscillates: its ordinate has maxima and minima, and its curvature changes sign infinitely often. Any arc AY is the equilibrium shape of a heavy lamina of length AY with top A free.

Previous page (§4): if the lower end Y is a point of vertical tangent (extremum of the ordinate), the lamina must be clamped into the floor along its direction.

This page:
- §4 concludes that, so clamped, the upper part takes the assigned figure under its own weight and stays in equilibrium.
- §5: at the points O where the curvature vanishes (inflection points), the bending moment is zero. So if the lower end is taken at such a point O', the lamina need not be clamped; it may simply stand on the floor EF (a pin with no moment).
- The free top transmits no horizontal force, so zero moment at O' means the centre of gravity G of the whole bent lamina O'NGMA lies on the vertical through O'.
- Euler notes this equilibrium is labile (unstable): the slightest force topples it, like an inverted rigid body balanced on a point.
- §6: none of these free-top cases fits the actual question. There both ends of the column must stay on the same vertical line, so the top A is not free. Euler therefore changes the initial state: besides gravity, an unknown horizontal force acts at A to keep it on the vertical through the base. Its size is found only at the end of the calculation.
- The next page sets up the auxiliary problem. Both ends are held on the vertical, a small horizontal force Cc acts at the middle C, and the critical case is the one where the deflection survives as Cc → 0, i.e. the pinned–pinned heavy column treated as an eigenvalue problem.
errors: No mathematical error on this page. The zero-moment / centre-of-gravity argument for a lamina simply resting at an inflection point is correct, given that the free top carries no horizontal force.
The original prints '§. 6.' twice: once here and again at 'Status Quaestionis' on the next page. This is a typographical numbering error in the printed edition.

ideas.what: Points of vertical tangent of the heavy-lamina curve correspond to clamped bases; inflection points (zero curvature, hence zero bending moment) correspond to bases that merely rest on the floor (pinned/simply supported).
ideas.modern_name: Correspondence between boundary conditions and zero moment/slope conditions; zero-moment points as hinge locations (segmenting an eigenfunction into sub-problems)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (implicit already in his 1744 elastica treatment of inflection points as hinge points)
ideas.where_published: E65 Additamentum I (1744) for the weightless elastica; here applied to the heavy column in E508–E510 (1778/1780)

ideas.what: Equilibrium of a buckled heavy lamina resting on a point is possible only if its centre of gravity lies vertically above the support, and such equilibrium is unstable (labile).
ideas.modern_name: Static equilibrium / instability of a pin-supported free-standing heavy column (inverted-pendulum type instability)

ideas.what: Reformulating the critical self-weight problem for a column with both ends held on the vertical: add an unknown horizontal end reaction at A, apply a small lateral disturbing force Cc, and find when deflection persists as Cc→0.
ideas.modern_name: Eigenvalue (bifurcation) formulation of self-weight buckling of a pinned–pinned heavy column, with redundant reaction determined by boundary conditions
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (E510); clamped–free case later definitively by Greenhill (1881) via Bessel functions
ideas.where_published: E510 (Acta Acad. Sci. Imp. Petropol. 1778, publ. 1780); discussed in Truesdell's historical account of elastic bodies (Opera omnia II 11/2)

deep.surprise_reason: This page sets up a known problem. It interprets the self-weight elastic curve, observes that a lamina can rest simply at an inflection point in labile equilibrium, and introduces the unknown end reaction. All of this is part of the documented history of Euler's heavy-column work (Truesdell). Nothing appears to be missing from the literature.
